summary: John's 10th-great-grandfather; founder and patentee of Smithtown on Long Island, known as Bull Smith.
bio:
Richard Smith, remembered as Bull Smith or the Patentee, was born in England about 1613. Of his earlier life, as one historian wrote, 'we know absolutely nothing'; some have said he came from a village in Yorkshire, but the evidence is thin. The most probable identification is with the Richard Smith who sailed from England on 2 October 1635, aged 22, in the ship John of London bound for St. Christophers, and his court-hand script suggests he was brought up in London. The Gloucestershire origin once given to him belongs to a different Richard Smith of Rhode Island, and a Bedfordshire origin has no source. The parents sometimes assigned to him, Sir Samuel Smith and Rebecca Buswell, are unsupported. Family tradition says his father used the blunderbuss 'Old Crib' in Cromwell's wars.

In April 1640, in Massachusetts Bay, 'Mr. Smith' petitioned to be released from his published intention to marry Sarah Hammond; he lost, and the marriage went ahead. His wife was Sarah Hammond, not the Sarah Folger of Boston given in older accounts. His first home lot at Southampton on Long Island, in the early 1640s, lay 'at the south end of the village, on the west side of the main street'. He probably went back to England in 1654 and returned in 1656 aboard the Speedwell with the first Quaker missionaries to New England, though this is debated; Southampton later banished him.

Smithtown came to him through Lion Gardiner, who had received the land for helping to recover the kidnapped daughter of Sachem Wyandanch and sold it to Smith in 1663; a patent of 1665 confirmed Smith's claim. The story that he won the land by riding a bull around it in a day is, according to local historians, a myth. He was styled Major Richard Smith, and his deeds of 1688, made as 'Gent.' with his wife Sarah, gave his son Job fifty acres at the northeast branch. His children were Jonathan, the eldest, whose daughter Deborah married Joseph Blydenburgh; Richard 2d; Job; Daniel; Adam, born in 1649; Elizabeth, who married William Lawrence, Governor Philip Carteret and Col. Richard Townley; and Deborah, who married Maj. William Lawrence Jr. He died at Smithtown in 1692. He was John's 10th-great-grandfather.
funFacts: The bull-ride legend of Smithtown's founding is a myth.
Tried to back out of marrying Sarah Hammond in 1640 and lost.
May have sailed home in 1656 on the same ship as the first Quaker missionaries to New England.

researchNotes:
Origin unknown. Pelletreau (1898, Intro. p. vii): 'Of his previous history we know absolutely nothing… He is said, by some historians, to have come from a certain village in Yorkshire, but the evidence is not sufficient.' F. K. Smith (1967, pp. 15–20): 'It now appears most probable that he was the Richard Smith who sailed from England 2 Oct. 1635, aged 22 years, in the ship John of London, bound for St. Christophers'; from his 'court hand' script, 'in all probability he was brought up in London'; probably unmarried before emigrating (speculative). WikiTree Smith-1208: parents unknown; 'Myreshaw, Bradford, Yorkshire' only as 'Unsourced information'; Y-DNA haplogroup R-b1, cluster NE50 of the SmithConnections project, no English match. Gloucestershire origin is disproven (belongs to Richard Smith of Cocumscussoc/Wickford, RI, earlier of Taunton, who 'left a fair possession in Gloucestershire'; both men died 1691/2, encouraging the merge). Bedfordshire origin: no source; probably cross-wired with Capt. Thomas Topping of Totternhoe. In April 1640 'Mr. Smith' petitioned to be released from his published intention to marry Sarah Hammond; Rev. George Phillips (and William Paine) wrote to Gov. Winthrop on 24 Apr 1640 about 'Smith & my brother Hammond dauter'; he lost and the marriage went ahead. His first home lot at Southampton (1640/1643) was 'at the south end of the village… on the west side of the main street'. F. K. Smith accepts he went back to England in 1654 and returned in 1656 aboard the Speedwell with the first Quaker missionaries to New England (not marked 'Q' on the list); Southampton later banished him (probable that the two Richards are the same; debated). Smithtown: Lion Gardiner received the land for helping recover Sachem Wyandanch's kidnapped daughter, sold it to Smith in 1663; a 1665 patent confirmed Smith's claim. The story that he won Smithtown by riding a bull around it is a myth per local historians. His 1688 deed gave Job 50 acres at the northeast branch. Children: Jonathan (eldest; daughter Deborah m. Joseph Blydenburgh), Richard 2d, Job, Daniel, Adam (b. 1649), Elizabeth (m. William Lawrence, Gov. Philip Carteret, Col. Richard Townley), Deborah (m. Maj. William Lawrence Jr.). TREE: 'Maj R B Sm(y)ith 1613–1692', parents 'Sir Samuel Smith 1575–1618 + Rebecca Buswell 1593–1667' — unsupported, removed (Round 1 correction 3d). His wife was formerly given as 'Sarah Folger of Boston' (Pelletreau) — corrected to Sarah Hammond (NYGBR 121).

Pelletreau's 1688 deeds (pp. 56-58, 71) show Richard Smith Sr. 'Gent.' with wife Sarah, acknowledged before Wait Winthrop ([R4-S1]); already in the tree in substance.
